mainTopic: נקדימון's miracles, the sun breaking through for משה, and רב יהודה's harsh פסוקים read as blessings (the reed and the cedar)
overview: The amud finishes the story of נקדימון בן גוריון. He prays in the בית המקדש and rain fills the twelve cisterns he borrowed for the עולי רגלים. When the official claims the sun had already set, נקדימון prays again and the sun breaks through, so his real name בוני became נקדימון. A ברייתא lists three people for whom the sun broke through: משה, יהושע and נקדימון. Three אמוראים then show where we learn it about משה. The גמרא returns to the משנה about a city without rain, and רב says both cities are cursed. This opens a series of רב יהודה's readings that turn harsh פסוקים into ברכות: ירושלים as a נדה, as a widow, Israel as lowly, and Israel as a reed. The reed that bends and survives is contrasted with בלעם's stiff cedar. A ברייתא teaches that a person should be soft like a reed. A story about רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, proud of his learning, begins and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Two men, two moods: the official at the bathhouse, נקדימון in the Temple
steps.stepSummary: The official mocks the idea of rain and goes happily to the bathhouse. At the same moment, נקדימון goes sadly to the בית המקדש to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: The official thought: 'Now, at the very end of the day, it is going to rain?!' He went into the bathhouse happy. While the official went happily into the bathhouse, נקדימון went into the בית המקדש sad. He wrapped himself in his טלית and stood to pray.
steps.whatsHappening: The story sets up two scenes side by side. The official is celebrating because he expects to collect the money, and נקדימון is turning to prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'while... at the same time' join the two scenes together. One man trusts in the calendar and the deadline. The other trusts in תפלה. This contrast is the background for the miracle that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The official or ruler (here, the Roman official who lent the water)
He wrapped himself (in his טלית, to pray)

phrases.english: And now it is going to rain?!
He entered the bathhouse in joy.
While the official was entering
the bathhouse in his joy,
Nakdimon entered the Temple
while he was sad.
He wrapped himself and stood in prayer.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַכְשָׁיו יֵרְדוּ גְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the נקדימון story begun earlier on the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The scene is set: the official celebrates, and נקדימון turns to תפלה.

steps.title: נקדימון's first prayer brings rain
steps.stepSummary: נקדימון tells הקדוש ברוך הוא that he acted only for His honor, so the pilgrims would have water. Right away rain fills the cisterns until they overflow.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said before God: Master of the World! You know clearly that I did not do this for my own honor, and not for the honor of my father's family. I did it for Your honor, so that there would be water for the עולי רגלים. Right away the sky filled with clouds, and rain fell until the twelve cisterns were full of water and even overflowed.
steps.whatsHappening: נקדימון prays, and the rain comes immediately and fills the cisterns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His prayer stresses one thing: his motive was pure, for the sake of Heaven and the pilgrims. The answer is even more than he needed. The cisterns overflow, which is why he will soon ask the official to pay for the extra water.

keyTerms.meaning: It is revealed and known before You
Pilgrims who come up to ירושלים for the festivals
The sky was tied up with clouds (it became cloudy)

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the World!
It is revealed and known before You
that I did not act for my own honor,
and I did not act for the honor of my father's house,
rather I acted for Your honor,
so that water would be available for the festival pilgrims.
Immediately the sky became covered with clouds,
and rain fell until they were filled
the twelve cisterns with water, and they overflowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the content of the prayer begun in step 1 and its answer
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A prayer said purely for the sake of Heaven is answered at once, and even beyond what was needed.

steps.title: The official's new claim: the sun already set
steps.stepSummary: נקדימון asks the official to pay for the extra water. The official admits the rain was a miracle for נקדימון, but says the deadline had already passed at sunset, so he can still take the silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as the official came out of the bathhouse, נקדימון בן גוריון came out of the בית המקדש. When they met, נקדימון said: 'Pay me for the extra water you got from me!' The official answered: 'I know that הקדוש ברוך הוא shook His world only for you. But I still have a claim against you that lets me take my money. The sun had already set, so the rain fell when the water was already mine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The two men meet, and the official raises a new legal argument to keep the money even after the miracle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The official does not deny the miracle. He argues about timing instead. The deal had a deadline, and he says the deadline passed at sunset. So the rain came too late, and the silver belongs to him. This sets up a second problem that only a second miracle can solve.

keyTerms.meaning: An opening of the mouth, meaning a claim or argument
Shook (here: stirred up the world with rain)

phrases.english: As the official came out of the bathhouse,

phrases.aramaic: נַקְדִּימוֹן בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן יָצָא מִבֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ.
phrases.english: Nakdimon ben Guryon came out of the Temple.
When they met each other, he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: תֵּן לִי דְּמֵי מַיִם יוֹתֵר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ!
phrases.english: Give me the money for the extra water that you owe me!
phrases.notes: The cisterns overflowed. So נקדימון says the official now has more water than he lent, and should pay for the extra.

phrases.english: He said to him: I know

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא הִרְעִישׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת עוֹלָמוֹ
phrases.english: that the Holy One, Blessed be He, did not shake His world
except for you,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה עָלֶיךָ,
phrases.english: but I still have a claim against you,
by which I can take my money from you,
because the sun has already set,
and the rain fell on my property.
phrases.notes: He means that the deadline was over, so the water already counted as his when the rain fell.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לִי פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה עָלֶיךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a new problem in the story after the rain miracle
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inside the story, the official argues that the deadline passed at sunset, so the payment is still owed to him.

steps.title: The second prayer: the sun breaks through
steps.stepSummary: נקדימון prays again, asking הקדוש ברוך הוא to show that He has beloved ones. The clouds scatter and the sun shines, and the official admits his claim is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: נקדימון went back into the בית המקדש, wrapped himself and stood in prayer. He said: Master of the World! Let it be known that You have beloved ones in Your world! Right away the clouds scattered and the sun shone. At that moment the official said to him: 'If the sun had not broken through, I would have had a claim against you to take my money.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second miracle answers the official's timing claim. The sun appears, which shows the day was not over yet.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The official claimed the sun had set. The sun now shines, so the deadline had not passed and his argument falls apart. He himself admits it. This time נקדימון's prayer asks for something different: he asks God to show openly that He loves those who serve Him.

keyTerms.meaning: Broke through (the sun burst out from behind the clouds)

phrases.english: He went back and entered the Temple,
wrapped himself and stood in prayer,
and said before Him: Master of the World!
Make known that You have beloved ones in Your world!
Immediately the clouds scattered and the sun shone.

phrases.aramaic: בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה אָמַר לוֹ אוֹתוֹ הֶגְמוֹן:
phrases.english: At that moment that official said to him:
Had the sun not broken through,
phrases.notes: Pay attention to the word נקדרה. The very next line builds his name from it.

phrases.english: I would have had a claim against you
by which I could take my money from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: חָזַר וְנִכְנַס לְבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the official's timing claim from step 3 through a second miracle
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sun reappears, which proves the deadline had not passed, and the official admits his claim is gone.
steps.whatToRemember: There were two miracles for נקדימון: first rain for the water, then the sun breaking through so the deadline had not passed.

steps.title: Why he was called נקדימון
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that his real name was בוני. He was called נקדימון because the sun 'broke through' (נקדרה) for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא taught: His name was not נקדימון. His name was בוני. Why was he called נקדימון? Because the sun broke through for his sake.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with a teaching that explains where נקדימון's name came from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name נקדימון is tied to the word נקדרה from the previous step. So the name itself is a reminder of the second miracle. This closes the story by linking his identity to the moment the sun broke through.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught (introduces a teaching from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: It was taught: Nakdimon was not his name,
rather Buni was his name,
and why was he called Nakdimon?
Because the sun broke through for his sake.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: לֹא נַקְדִּימוֹן שְׁמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the word נקדרה from step 4 to explain the name
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: נקדימון's real name was בוני. His famous name records the miracle that the sun broke through for him.
steps.whatToRemember: נקדימון = נקדרה חמה: his name is a lasting sign of the miracle of the sun.

steps.title: Three people for whom the sun broke through
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the sun broke through for three people: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: There were three people for whom the sun broke through for their sake: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that groups נקדימון together with two great figures, משה and יהושע. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story we just finished ended with the sun breaking through for נקדימון. Now the ברייתא says this miracle happened to only three people in history. Putting נקדימון next to משה and יהושע shows how great his miracle was.

keyTerms.meaning: The sun broke through / shone early for them

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Three people, for whom the sun broke through for their sake:
Moshe, Yehoshua, and Nakdimon ben Guryon.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שְׁלֹשָׁה נִקְדְּמָה לָהֶם חַמָּה בַּעֲבוּרָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the miracle of the sun breaking through for נקדימון by listing the other people it happened to.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sun broke through miraculously for exactly three people: משה, יהושע, and נקדימון בן גוריון.

steps.title: How do we know the sun broke through for משה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts נקדימון (known from the story) and יהושע (known from a פסוק), but asks for the source for משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We understand נקדימון בן גוריון, because we know it from the story we learned. We also understand יהושע, because a פסוק says: 'And the sun stood still and the moon stayed.' But how do we know it about משה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks each name on the list and finds a source for two of them. It asks where we see this for משה, and this sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For נקדימון we have the story, and for יהושע a פסוק in ספר יהושע says the sun stood still. But no פסוק openly says the sun stood still for משה. So the גמרא wants to know what the ברייתא is based on.

phrases.english: Granted, Nakdimon ben Guryon — we know it from tradition.
phrases.notes: 'גמרא' here means the story we just learned about him, not the Talmud itself.

phrases.english: Yehoshua too — we know it from a verse,
as it is written: "And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, etc."
But Moshe, from where do we know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא נַקְדִּימוֹן בֶּן גּוּרְיוֹן גְּמָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind one of the three names in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that the sun broke through for משה.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: learned from the word 'I will begin'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר learns it through a גזירה שוה on the word 'אחל', which is used both for משה and for יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: We learn it from 'אחל' (I will begin) and 'אחל'. Here, about משה, it says: 'I will begin to put the dread of you.' And there, about יהושע, it says: 'I will begin to make you great.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives the first answer. He links a פסוק about משה to a פסוק about יהושע because both use the same word 'אחל'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the same word appears in both places, what happened to one happened to the other. The sun stood still for יהושע, so it must have done the same for משה. This is a גזירה שוה, a link between two פסוקים through a shared word.

keyTerms.meaning: It is learned (through a link between פסוקים)
It is written here... and it is written there (formula of a גזירה שוה)

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
It is learned from "I will begin" and "I will begin."
It is written here: "I will begin to put the dread of you,"
and it is written there: "I will begin to make you great."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אָתְיָא ״אָחֵל״ ״אָחֵל״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on 'אחל' links משה to יהושע, so the sun stood still for משה too.

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני: learned from the word 'to put'
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני uses a different word-link, 'תת', which ties משה's פסוק directly to the day the sun stood still for יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said: We learn it from 'תת' (to put) and 'תת'. Here, about משה, it says: 'I will begin to put the dread of you.' And there it says: 'On the day when ה׳ put the Amorites.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a different answer to the same question. He uses the word 'תת' instead of 'אחל'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His 'there' פסוק is the actual day the sun stood still for יהושע (fighting the Amorites). So his link connects משה straight to the sun miracle itself, not just to יהושע in general.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said:
It is learned from "to put" and "to put."
It is written here: "I will begin to put the dread of you,"

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב הָתָם: ״בְּיוֹם תֵּת ה׳ אֶת הָאֱמֹרִי״.
phrases.english: and it is written there: "On the day when the Lord put the Amorites."
phrases.notes: יהושע 10:12, the same day יהושע told the sun to stand still.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר: אָתְיָא ״תֵּת״ ״תֵּת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to step 7, using a different shared word than רבי אלעזר.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה on 'תת' links משה's פסוק to the day the sun stood still for יהושע.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: learned from the verse about משה itself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says no word-link is needed. The פסוק about משה itself says the nations would tremble, and that happened when the sun broke through for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: We learn it from the פסוק itself: 'Who will hear the report of you, and tremble, and be in anguish because of you.' When did they tremble and shake because of you? At the time the sun broke through for משה.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא answers the question without comparing to יהושע at all. He reads it from the end of the same פסוק about משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק promises that all the nations under heaven will hear about משה and shake. רבי יוחנן asks what event could make the whole world tremble, and answers that it was the sun breaking through for משה. So the miracle is hinted in משה's own פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: And they will tremble and be in anguish

steps.whatToRemember: There are three sources for the sun breaking through for משה: רבי אלעזר links 'אחל' to יהושע, רבי שמואל בר נחמני links 'תת' to the day of the sun miracle, and רבי יוחנן reads it from משה's own פסוק, which says the nations trembled.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is learned from the verse itself:
phrases.notes: He means the same פסוק about משה, דברים 2:25, read further on.

phrases.english: "Who will hear the report of you,
and will tremble and be in anguish because of you."
When did they tremble and were in anguish because of you?
At the time the sun broke through for Moshe.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר, אָתְיָא מִגּוּפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a third answer to step 7, reading the source directly from משה's פסוק instead of using a word-link.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The nations trembled before משה, as the פסוק says, when the sun broke through for him.

steps.title: A city without rain: both cities are cursed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about one city that gets no rain, and רב יהודה in the name of רב says both cities suffer a קללה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And likewise, a city that got no rain, etc.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: both cities, the one without rain and the one with rain, are under a קללה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and opens a new topic: a city that got no rain while its neighbor did. רב says that both cities are being punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think the city that got rain is the lucky one. רב says no: both cities are under a קללה. Going by the פסוק in עמוס, one city dries out, and the other may get rain that does damage. The next steps bring more teachings from the same רב יהודה that read פסוקים against their simple meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: A city that did not get rain
Short for 'etc.': the rest of the quote from the משנה
Both of them, meaning both cities

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁלֹּא יָרְדוּ עָלֶיהָ גְּשָׁמִים כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: And likewise, a city upon which rain did not fall, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה, which is based on עמוס 4:7.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
And both of them are for a curse.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁלֹּא יָרְדוּ עָלֶיהָ גְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story of the sun breaking through and goes back to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When one city gets rain and another does not, both cities are under a קללה.

steps.title: Jerusalem like a נדה: she will become permitted again
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, in the name of רב, reads the פסוק comparing ירושלים to a נדה as a ברכה: just as a נדה becomes permitted again, ירושלים will be rebuilt.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'ירושלים among them was like a נדה.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: this is a ברכה. Just as a נדה will become permitted to her husband again, ירושלים will be repaired.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching of רב יהודה in the name of רב. Here a פסוק that sounds like a קללה is read as a ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the step before, רב turned something that sounded like a ברכה into a קללה. Here it goes the other way. The comparison to a נדה is not only about being separated. A נדה's time apart ends, and then she becomes permitted again. In the same way, ירושלים's destruction is not forever.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman during her monthly time of separation from her husband
For a blessing, meaning this is really good news
A way to become permitted again
A repair, a fixing. Here it means rebuilding.

phrases.english: "Jerusalem among them was like a menstruating woman"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לִבְרָכָה,
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said: It is for a blessing,

phrases.aramaic: כְּנִדָּה: מָה נִדָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ הֶיתֵּר
phrases.english: like a menstruating woman: just as a menstruating woman has a way to become permitted,
so too, Jerusalem has a repair.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לִבְרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another reading by the same רב יהודה in the name of רב that goes against the simple meaning of a פסוק. This time a קללה is turned into a ברכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comparing ירושלים to a נדה promises that her destruction will end and she will be rebuilt.

steps.title: Jerusalem like a widow: her husband plans to come back
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reads 'she became like a widow' as a ברכה: ירושלים is only like a widow, like a wife whose husband went overseas and plans to return.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'She became like a widow.' רב יהודה said: this is a ברכה. It says 'like' a widow, not a real widow. She is like a woman whose husband went to a faraway land and plans to come back to her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third teaching of רב יהודה that turns a sad פסוק into a ברכה. This time the reading hangs on the small letter כ, 'like'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is the word כְּ, 'like'. A real widow's husband is gone forever. A woman whose husband is far away only looks like a widow, and he means to come home. So ירושלים is not abandoned for good; הקב"ה plans to return to her.

keyTerms.meaning: A land across the sea, a faraway place

steps.confusionAlert: Don't miss the small letter כְּ ('like') in כְּאַלְמָנָה. The whole ברכה comes from that one letter: she only seems to be a widow.

phrases.english: "She has become like a widow"
Rav Yehuda said: It is for a blessing:
like a widow, and not a real widow,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כְּאִשָּׁה שֶׁהָלַךְ בַּעְלָהּ לִמְדִינַת הַיָּם,
phrases.english: but rather like a woman whose husband went to a country overseas,
and he intends to return to her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה, לִבְרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of רב יהודה's teachings that read a sad פסוק about ירושלים as a ברכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ירושלים is only 'like' a widow. Her 'husband' is away for now, but he plans to return.

steps.title: Looked down on, but spared the worst jobs
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה reads 'I made you contemptible and lowly' as a ברכה: because the nations look down on us, they don't appoint us to their hated official jobs.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'I have also made you contemptible and lowly.' רב יהודה said: this is a ברכה. Because they think little of us, they don't make us river officials or government officials.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching in this list. רב יהודה finds a good side to being looked down on by the nations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being seen as lowly sounds only bad. But because of it, the rulers don't push Jews into their official jobs, like river officials and government officials. So the 'shame' in the פסוק actually protects us.

keyTerms.meaning: They appoint, they put into a job

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה has a pattern of reading פסוקים against their simple meaning. Something that sounds like a ברכה can hide a קללה (both cities are cursed). And harsh פסוקים can hide ברכות: ירושלים is like a נדה who will become permitted again, like a widow whose husband will come back, and we are looked down on but spared the worst jobs. The next steps add one more: ישראל compared to a reed.

phrases.english: "And I have also made you contemptible and base"
Rav Yehuda said: It is for a blessing,
for they do not appoint from among us
either river officials or government officials.
phrases.notes: These were jobs no one wanted, so being passed over for them is a good thing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: לִבְרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another in the list of רב יהודה's readings that find a ברכה in a harsh פסוק. The list continues in step 15 with the reed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being looked down on by the nations has a good side: they do not appoint Jews to their unwanted official jobs.

steps.title: The reed shaken in water is really a blessing
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says that אחיה השילוני's words, 'ה׳ will strike Israel like a reed swaying in water,' are actually a ברכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And ה׳ will strike Israel as the reed sways in the water.' רב יהודה said in the name of רב: this is for a blessing.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the next item in רב יהודה's list of harsh-sounding פסוקים that are really ברכות. Here he quotes the prophet אחיה השילוני comparing ישראל to a reed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the surface, being struck and shaken like a reed sounds like a punishment. רב יהודה says the comparison hides a blessing. The next step brings the source that explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: A reed, a thin plant that grows in water

phrases.english: "And the LORD will strike Israel
phrases.notes: מלכים א 14:15. These are the words of the prophet אחיה השילוני.

phrases.english: as the reed sways in the water"
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
It is for a blessing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר רב יהודה אמר רב לברכה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב יהודה's series of curses read as blessings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אחיה השילוני's comparison of ישראל to a reed is really a ברכה.

steps.title: A friend's curse is better than an enemy's blessing
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, in the name of רבי יונתן, explains a פסוק in משלי: אחיה השילוני's curse is better than בלעם's blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: What does the פסוק mean, 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful'? The curse that אחיה השילוני cursed ישראל with is better than the blessing that בלעם the wicked blessed them with.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for רב יהודה's reading. It quotes a teaching that a curse from someone who loves you is better than a blessing from someone who hates you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אחיה was a true prophet who cared about ישראל, so even his 'wounds' are honest and helpful. בלעם hated ישראל, so even his 'kisses' were a trick. The next steps show exactly how this plays out with the reed and the cedar.

keyTerms.meaning: A prophet from the time of ירבעם
בלעם the wicked, the non-Jewish prophet who tried to curse ישראל

phrases.english: As Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"Faithful are the wounds of a friend,
but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful"?
Better is the curse
with which Ahijah the Shilonite cursed Israel
than the blessing
with which Balaam the wicked blessed them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דאמר רבי שמואל בר נחמני אמר רבי יונתן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source backing רב יהודה's claim that the reed comparison is a blessing.
steps.raayaObject: That אחיה's reed 'curse' is really a ברכה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in משלי about a friend's wounds and an enemy's kisses, as explained by רבי יונתן.

steps.title: Why the reed is a blessing
steps.stepSummary: The reed grows by water, regrows when cut, has many roots, and bends with every wind without being pulled out. When the winds stop, it is still standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחיה השילוני cursed them with a reed. He said to ישראל‎: 'ה׳ will strike Israel as the reed sways.' Just as this reed stands in a place of water, its stem grows back, and its roots are many, and even if all the winds in the world come and blow at it, they cannot move it from its place. Instead, it sways back and forth with them. When the winds go quiet, the reed is still standing in its place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first half of the contrast: what is so good about being compared to a reed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reed has water, it renews itself, and it holds on strongly with many roots. Its secret is that it bends instead of fighting the wind, so nothing can uproot it. The hint is that ישראל will be pushed around by troubles but will survive and stay in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Its stem grows back after being cut

phrases.english: Ahijah the Shilonite cursed them with a reed;
he said to Israel:

phrases.aramaic: ״וְהִכָּה ה׳ אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל כַּאֲשֶׁר יָנוּד הַקָּנֶה״,
phrases.english: "And the LORD will strike Israel as the reed sways."
Just as this reed
stands in a place of water,
and its stem grows back,
and its roots are many,
and even if all the winds in the world
come and blow against it,
they do not move it from its place;
rather, it sways back and forth with them.
Once the winds go quiet,
the reed is still standing in its place.

steps.triggerLanguage: אחיה השילוני קיללן בקנה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the first half of רבי יונתן's comparison: the reed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reed bends with the winds but is never uprooted, a picture of ישראל surviving every trouble.

steps.title: Why the cedar is a weaker blessing
steps.stepSummary: בלעם compared ישראל to cedars. A cedar has no water, does not regrow, and has few roots. It stands strong until the south wind knocks it over. And the reed even gets used as a quill to write the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But בלעם the wicked blessed them with a cedar, as it says, 'Like cedars by the water.' Just as this cedar does not stand in a place of water, its stem does not grow back, and its roots are not many. Even if all the winds in the world blow at it, they cannot move it from its place. But once the south wind blows at it, it uproots it and flips it on its face. And not only that, the reed earned that a quill is taken from it to write a ספר תורה, נביאים, and כתובים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the contrast by showing the weak points of the cedar that בלעם chose. It ends with one more advantage of the reed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cedar looks mighty, but it is stiff, so one strong wind can tear it out by the roots. בלעם's 'blessing' hid a wish for ישראל to fall all at once. The reed also earns the honor of becoming a pen for holy writing, so the friend's 'curse' really is better.

keyTerms.meaning: A cedar tree, tall and stiff

steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק says the cedars are 'by the water,' yet the גמרא says a cedar does NOT stand in a place of water. The גמרא is describing what a real cedar is like, and those real traits are the cedar's weaknesses compared to the reed.
steps.whatToRemember: A friend's 'curse' (the bending reed) beats an enemy's 'blessing' (the stiff cedar). The reed survives every storm and even becomes the pen for writing the תורה.

phrases.english: But Balaam the wicked blessed them with a cedar,
as it is stated: "Like cedars beside the waters."
Just as this cedar
does not stand in a place of water,
and its stem does not grow back,
and its roots are not many.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ כׇּל הָרוּחוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם נוֹשְׁבוֹת בּוֹ
phrases.english: Even if all the winds in the world blow against it,
they do not move it from its place.
But once the south wind blows against it,
it uproots it and turns it over on its face.
And not only that, but
the reed merited that a quill is taken from it

phrases.aramaic: לִכְתּוֹב בּוֹ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה נְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים.
phrases.english: to write with it a Torah scroll, the Prophets, and the Writings.

steps.triggerLanguage: אבל בלעם הרשע בירכן בארז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the other side of the contrast, the cedar, and closes the comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cedar seems strong but falls to one wind, while the reed survives and is even used to write holy books, so אחיה's 'curse' is better than בלעם's 'blessing.'

steps.title: Be soft like a reed, not hard like a cedar
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a person should always be soft and bendable like a reed, not stiff like a cedar.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A person should always be soft like a reed and should not be hard like a cedar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that turns the reed-and-cedar picture into a lesson about how a person should behave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the reed and cedar were about the fate of the Jewish people. Now they become advice for each person: be flexible and humble, not stiff and proud. The story that follows will show this lesson in action.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person should always be soft like a reed
and should not be hard like a cedar.

steps.triggerLanguage: תנו רבנן לעולם יהא אדם רך כקנה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the reed and cedar image and turns it into a lesson about personal character.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should always be soft and flexible like a reed, not stiff like a cedar.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון rides home feeling proud
steps.stepSummary: A story begins: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was coming home from his teacher, riding a donkey by the river, very happy and feeling proud because he had learned so much תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an incident in which רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון came from מגדל גדור, from his teacher's house. He was riding on a donkey and strolling along the riverbank. He was very happy, and he felt full of himself because he had learned a lot of תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story to illustrate the lesson of being soft like a reed. This step only sets the scene; the main event comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story points out that רבי אלעזר was feeling proud. That is the 'hard like a cedar' attitude the ברייתא just warned against. The learner should expect the next part to show what went wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: His teacher's house, where he learned
He felt proud, full of himself

phrases.english: There was an incident in which there came
Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon,
from Migdal Gedor, from the house of his teacher,
and he was riding on a donkey
and strolling along the bank of the river,
and he was very happy.
And he was feeling proud
phrases.notes: Literally, 'his mind was coarse upon him.' It means he was full of himself.

phrases.english: because he had learned much Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: מעשה שבא רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון ממגדל גדור
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a story that will illustrate the ברייתא's lesson about being soft like a reed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scene-setting: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון was proud of his learning, the cedar-like attitude the story will go on to correct.
